question.text:
According to the Chinese remainder theorem, which of the following systems of congruences has a unique solution modulo $60?$

\[ \text{I.}\: \begin{cases} x \equiv 1 & (\text{mod}\:3) \\ x \equiv 2 & (\text{mod}\:4) \\ x \equiv 3 & (\text{mod}\:5) \\ \end{cases} \qquad \text{II.}\: \begin{cases} x \equiv 3 & (\text{mod}\:6) \\ x \equiv 2 & (\text{mod}\:10) \end{cases} \qquad \text{III.}\: \begin{cases} x \equiv 2 & (\text{mod}\:5) \\ x \equiv 3 & (\text{mod}\:12) \\ \end{cases} \qquad \]
question.explanation:
The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers $n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}(n_i,n_j)=1$ whenever $i \neq j,$ then for any integers $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k$ the system

\[ \begin{cases} x \equiv a_1 & (\text{mod}\:n_1) \\ x \equiv a_2 & (\text{mod}\:n_2) \\ \quad\vdots \\ x \equiv a_k & (\text{mod}\:n_k) \\ \end{cases} \]

has a unique solution modulo $n_1 n_2 \cdots n_k.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

  • The theorem applies to system I. The numbers $3,$ $4,$ and $5$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 = 60.$

  • The theorem does not apply to system II since $6$ and $10$ are not coprime: \[ \text{gcd}(6,10)=2 > 1 \]

  • The theorem applies to system III. The numbers $5$ and $12$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $5 \cdot 12 = 60.$

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

question.text: Find the smallest natural number solution to the system of linear congruences below. \[ \begin{cases} x \equiv 1 & (\text{mod}\:3) \\ x \equiv 3 & (\text{mod}\:4) \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
Since $3$ and $4$ are coprime, then according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3 \cdot 4 = 12.$

From the first congruence, we get

\[ x \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:3) \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = 1 + 3t, \quad t \in \mathbb{Z}. \]

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:4) \\[3pt] 1 + 3t &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:4) \\[3pt] 3t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:4) \end{align*}

Since $4$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $3 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:4).$ So, we multiply both sides by $3\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:4) \\[3pt] 3 \cdot 3t &\equiv 6 && \quad (\text{mod}\:4) \\[3pt] t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:4) \end{align*}

As a result, $t = 2 + 4s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} x &= 1 + 3t \\[3pt] &= 1 + 3(2+4s) \\[3pt] &= 7 + 12s. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x \equiv 7 \: (\text{mod}\:12)$ is the unique solution modulo $12,$ and $x=7$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

question.explanation:
Since $3,$ $5,$ and $11$ are coprime, then according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3 \cdot 5 \cdot 11 = 165.$

We will solve the system in two steps.

Step 1. Find the common solution for the first and second congruences of the system.

From the first congruence, we get

\[ x \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:3) \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = 3t, \quad t \in \mathbb{Z}. \]

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 4 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[5pt] 3t &\equiv 4 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Since $5$ is a relatively small modulus, we can solve it by trial and error. We have that $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:5).$ So, we multiply both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3t &\equiv 4 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[5pt] 2 \cdot 3t &\equiv 8 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[5pt] t &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \end{align*}

As a result, $t = 3 + 5s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

\begin{align*} x &= 3t \\[5pt] &= 3(3+5s) \\[5pt] &= 9 + 15s \end{align*}

Step 2. Find the common solution of all three congruences.

Now, substituting the common solution of the first two congruences into the third congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 10 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9 + 15s &\equiv 10 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 15s &\equiv 1 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 4s &\equiv 1 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11) \end{align*}

Since $11$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $3 \cdot 4 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:11).$ So, we multiply both sides by $3\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 4s &\equiv 1 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11)\\[5pt] 3 \cdot 4s &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11)\\[5pt] s &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:11) \end{align*}

As a result, $s = 3 + 11u,$ where $u \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

\begin{align*} x &= 9 + 15s \\[5pt] &= 9 + 15(3+11u) \\[5pt] &= 54 + 165u. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x \equiv 54 \: (\text{mod}\:165)$ is the unique solution modulo $165,$ and $x=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{54}$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

Since $7$ is a relatively small modulus, we can solve it by trial and error. We have that $5 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:7).$ So, we multiply both sides by $5\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 5 \cdot 3t &\equiv 10 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] t &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

As a result, $t = 3 + 7s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 5 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \\[3pt] 11 + 21s &\equiv 5 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \\[3pt] 21s &\equiv -6 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \\[3pt] 5s &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \end{align*}

\begin{align*} 5s &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \\[3pt] 5 \cdot 5s &\equiv 10 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \\[3pt] s &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:8) \end{align*}

As a result, $s = 2 + 8u,$ where $u \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:3) \\[3pt] 1 + 2t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:3) \\[3pt] 2t &\equiv 1 && \quad (\text{mod}\:3) \end{align*}

Since $3$ is a relatively small modulus, we can solve it by trial and error. We have that $2 \cdot 2 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:3).$ So, we multiply both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 2t &\equiv 1 && \quad (\text{mod}\:3) \\[3pt] 2 \cdot 2t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:3) \\[3pt] t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:3) \end{align*}

As a result, $t = 2 + 3s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

\begin{align*} x &= 1 + 2t \\[3pt] &= 1 + 2(2+3s) \\[3pt] &= 5 + 6s \end{align*}

Step 2. Find the common solution of all three congruences.

Now, substituting the common solution of the first two congruences into the third congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 5 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 5 + 6s &\equiv 5 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 6s &\equiv 0 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

Since $7$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $6 \cdot 6 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:7).$ Hence,

\begin{align*} 6s &\equiv 0 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 6\cdot 6s &\equiv 0 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] s &\equiv 0 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

As a result, $s = 7u,$ where $u \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

\begin{align*} x &= 5 + 6s \\[3pt] &= 5 + 6(7u) \\[3pt] &= 5 + 42u. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x \equiv 5 \: (\text{mod}\:42)$ is the unique solution modulo $42,$ and $x=5$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

example.title: Solving a System of Three Linear Congruences

question.text: Find the smallest natural number solution to the system of linear congruences below. \[ \begin{cases} x \equiv 1 & (\text{mod}\:2) \\ x \equiv 3 & (\text{mod}\:5) \\ x \equiv 5 & (\text{mod}\:7) \\ \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
Since $2,$ $5,$ and $7$ are coprime, then according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 70.$

We will solve the system in two steps.

Step 1. Find the common solution for the first and second congruences of the system.

From the first congruence, we get

\[ x \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:2) \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = 1 + 2t, \quad t \in \mathbb{Z}. \]

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] 1 + 2t &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] 2t &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] t &\equiv 1 && \quad (\text{mod}\:5) \end{align*}

As a result, $t = 1 + 5s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

\begin{align*} x &= 1 + 2t \\[3pt] &= 1 + 2(1+5s) \\[3pt] &= 3 + 10s \end{align*}

Step 2. Find the common solution of all three congruences.

Now, substituting the common solution of the first two congruences into the third congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x &\equiv 5 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 3 + 10s &\equiv 5 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 10s &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 3s &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

Since $7$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $5 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:7).$ So, we multiply both sides by $5\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3s &\equiv 2 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] 5 \cdot 3s &\equiv 10 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \\[3pt] s &\equiv 3 && \quad (\text{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

As a result, $s = 3 + 7u,$ where $u \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

\begin{align*} x &= 3 + 10s \\[3pt] &= 3 + 10(3+7u) \\[3pt] &= 33 + 70u. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x \equiv 33 \: (\text{mod}\:70)$ is the unique solution modulo $70,$ and $x=33$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.
